resource.title: Deep Learning — Real-world Case Study
resource.heroSubtitle: A production Deep Learning case study — from stakeholder analysis and dataset curation to PyTorch model design, deployment, monitoring, and measurable business impact.

html:
1. Company Overview

NovaRetail is a mid-market e-commerce company operating across 14 countries with roughly 9 million monthly active users. Their catalogue contains 1.4M SKUs across fashion, home, and electronics. In 2024, leadership committed to a Deep Learning initiative to replace brittle rule-based systems in personalisation, search, and inventory demand forecasting.

  • Industry: Consumer e-commerce.
  • Team: 6 ML engineers, 3 data engineers, 2 SREs, 1 product lead.
  • Stack: PyTorch 2.x, Ray, Feast, Triton Inference Server, Kubernetes.

2. Business Problem

Pain point

Product recommendations were generated by a hand-tuned collaborative filter refreshed nightly. CTR had plateaued at 3.1% for eight quarters and conversion on the recommender surface trailed the site average by 22%.

Three symptoms surfaced simultaneously:

  • Cold-start failure — new items got no meaningful exposure for 7+ days.
  • Session incoherence — the model ignored intra-session intent shifts.
  • Long tail collapse — 84% of impressions concentrated on the top 5% of SKUs.

3. Project Objectives

  • Ship a Deep Learning recommender lifting CTR by ≥15% and revenue-per-visit by ≥8%.
  • Support cold-start ranking within 30 minutes of catalogue ingest.
  • Serve p99 latency under 90ms at 12k requests/second at peak.
  • Maintain fairness across long-tail categories via exposure guardrails.

4. Requirement Analysis

Stakeholders: merchandising, product, SRE, legal (GDPR), and finance.

Requirement gathering happened over four workshops. Legal established that only hashed user IDs and behavioural events could be modelled; PII would never enter training data. SRE mandated horizontal scalability, blue-green deploys, and a rollback path under three minutes.

5. Dataset Collection

14 months of clickstream (impressions, clicks, add-to-cart, purchases), catalogue metadata (title, description, taxonomy, price, images), and merchandising signals (badges, promotions). Roughly 4.8B events and 1.4M items.

6. Data Preparation

Feature engineering pipelines were consolidated in Feast with three views:

  • User features: rolling engagement counts, embeddings of recent categories, freshness decay.
  • Item features: price percentile, availability, image CLIP embeddings, title/desc encoder embeddings.
  • Context features: device, hour, referrer, promo state.
code
# Two-tower features are precomputed nightly and streamed hot-path from Feast
user_features = fs.get_online_features(entity_rows=[{"user_id": uid}], features=USER_VIEW)
item_features = fs.get_online_features(entity_rows=[{"item_id": iid} for iid in candidates], features=ITEM_VIEW)

7. Model Architecture

A two-tower retrieval model with a shared 128-dim embedding space feeds a cross-attention ranker. Retrieval runs ANN over a FAISS index; the ranker re-orders the top 500 candidates.

code
class TwoTower(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d=128):
        super().__init__()
        self.user_encoder = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(USER_DIM, 512), nn.GELU(),
            nn.Linear(512, d),
        )
        self.item_encoder = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(ITEM_DIM, 512), nn.GELU(),
            nn.Linear(512, d),
        )

    def forward(self, u, i):
        u = F.normalize(self.user_encoder(u), dim=-1)
        i = F.normalize(self.item_encoder(i), dim=-1)
        return (u * i).sum(-1)

8. Training Strategy

  • Sampled softmax over 4k in-batch negatives + hard negatives from ANN.
  • Cosine LR schedule with 3% warmup, AdamW, bf16 on 8×A100.
  • Ranker fine-tuned with pairwise logistic loss weighted by conversion value.
  • Deterministic seeds, per-epoch offline eval on held-out sessions.

9. System Architecture

End-to-end topology:

Kafka events ─▶ Feature Store (Feast) ─▶ Training (Ray/PyTorch) ─▶ Model Registry
                          │                                               │
                          ▼                                               ▼
                 Online features ◀────────── Triton Ranker ◀──── FAISS Retrieval
                          │                          │
                          └────────────▶ API Gateway ▶ Storefront

10. Deployment Pipeline

Models are packaged as TorchScript, benchmarked against a golden traffic sample, then promoted through canary (1%) → shadow (25% mirrored) → full rollout. Every promotion gate is a pull-request check.

11. Monitoring & Maintenance

  • Prometheus for latency, QPS, memory, GPU utilisation.
  • Feature-drift PSI on top 40 features; alerts on PSI > 0.2.
  • Weekly counterfactual holdout comparing model vs previous champion.

12. Performance Evaluation

CTR3.1%3.9%+26%
RPV$1.42$1.61+13%
p99 latency140ms78ms-44%
Long-tail coverage16%34%+112%

13. Business Outcomes

} title="Impact">

Annualised revenue uplift of $34M, a 22-week payback on the platform investment, and merchandising time-to-launch reduced from 5 days to 40 minutes.

14. Lessons Learned

  • Data quality dominated model choice — three of the biggest wins came from labels, not layers.
  • Serving costs were dictated by the ranker, not the retriever — distillation was worth the effort.
  • Shadow deploys caught two silent regressions that offline metrics missed entirely.

15. Future Enhancements

  • Multimodal item towers using CLIP image embeddings and product-video summaries.
  • Session-level transformer ranker with RL fine-tuning against long-term reward.
  • On-device pre-fetch of top-N candidates to reduce cold-start latency further.

Real-world Review

Executive summary

DL delivered a step-change in ranking quality and reduced serving latency simultaneously — a rare combination that unlocked broader roadmap ambition.

Engineering takeaways

  • Feature store discipline pays for itself the first time you retrain.
  • Retrieval + ranker separation kept latency predictable at scale.
  • Canary + shadow deploys were the highest-ROI SRE investment.

Discussion questions

  • How would you re-scope this project for a team of two?
  • Which guardrails would you add to protect long-tail exposure?
  • Where would multimodal signals move the needle first?

Reflection activities

  • Draft an equivalent architecture diagram for a marketplace with only 20k items.
  • Sketch a rollback playbook for a mis-behaving canary at 2% traffic.

Industry insights

Two-tower + cross-attention ranker is the current default at most large recommender systems (Meta, Pinterest, Alibaba, Netflix). The differentiator is feature engineering and evaluation discipline, not architecture novelty.

Summary & Key Takeaways

  • Frame the business problem before choosing the model.
  • Feature stores, canaries, and drift monitoring make DL projects survivable.
  • Measurable outcomes — CTR, RPV, latency — are the only language leadership rewards.

FAQ

Why two-tower and not a single ranker?
Retrieval + ranker separates a fast approximate step from an expensive precise step, letting you scale independently.
How was cold-start solved?
Item towers depend only on catalogue features, so a new SKU is rankable the moment it lands in Feast.
Is TensorFlow a viable substitute?
Yes — the architecture is framework-agnostic. PyTorch was chosen for team familiarity and Triton compatibility.

Glossary

  • ANN — Approximate Nearest Neighbour search (e.g. FAISS, ScaNN).
  • PSI — Population Stability Index for feature drift.
  • RPV — Revenue Per Visit.
  • Triton — NVIDIA inference server supporting multi-framework model serving.
